title: Direct and Indirect Speech
tagline: Grammar · reporting statements, questions, commands and exclamations

sourceNote.boardprep: All rules, tables, example sentences, questions and answers on this page are original BoardPrep material written for practice and are not taken from any textbook, guide or past paper.

overview.intro: Direct speech repeats a speaker's exact words inside quotation marks. Indirect (reported) speech tells what was said without quoting, usually in a that clause or a question or command form joined to a reporting verb. Changing one into the other means adjusting the tense, pronouns, and words of time and place, and choosing a suitable reporting verb. Most errors arise from forgetting one of these changes, or from applying back-shift where it should not be applied.

facts.label: Direct speech
facts.value: Exact words in quotation marks: She said, 'I am tired.'

facts.label: Indirect speech
facts.value: Reported without quotation marks: She said that she was tired.

facts.label: Four sentence types
facts.value: Statements, questions, commands or requests, exclamations

facts.label: Four things to change
facts.value: Tense, pronouns, time and place words, reporting verb

facts.label: Exceptions
facts.value: Universal truths and reporting verbs in the present or future need no back-shift

blocks.text: The reporting verb (said, asked, told) and the words spoken (the reported speech) are the two parts of a sentence in speech. When the reporting verb is in a past tense, the reported words usually move one step back in time, which is called back-shift. The pronouns shift to fit the person who is now reporting, and words such as now, here and tomorrow shift to match the new viewpoint.

items.text: Direct: Ritu said, 'I am reading a novel.' Indirect: Ritu said that she was reading a novel.
items.note: I becomes she; am reading becomes was reading; the quotation marks and comma disappear and that is added.

items.meaning: For statements: said to becomes told (with the listener) or said (without): He said to me becomes He told me. For questions: asked. For commands: told, ordered, commanded. For requests: requested, asked. For advice: advised. For exclamations: exclaimed.

When the reporting verb is past: simple present becomes simple past; present continuous becomes past continuous; present perfect becomes past perfect; simple past becomes past perfect (or stays as simple past); will becomes would; can becomes could; may becomes might; shall becomes would or should.
Would, could, should, might and ought to do not change. Must stays as must when it shows a rule or a strong belief, and may become had to when it shows a past necessity.
First person pronouns change to match the subject of the reporting verb; second person pronouns change to match the listener; third person pronouns usually stay the same.

now becomes then; today becomes that day; tonight becomes that night; tomorrow becomes the next day or the following day; yesterday becomes the previous day or the day before; last week becomes the previous week; next week becomes the following week; ago becomes before; here becomes there; this becomes that; these becomes those; come becomes go where the direction changes.

Statements: add that. Yes or no questions: use if or whether. Wh-questions: keep the question word. Commands: use to plus the base verb (not to for negatives). Exclamations: use exclaimed with joy, sorrow or surprise, followed by that.
Use statement word order and no question mark. He asked, 'Where do you live?' becomes He asked where I lived.

blocks.text: When not to back-shift: (1) If the reporting verb is in the present or future (He says, 'I am busy.' becomes He says that he is busy), the tense of the reported words stays the same. (2) If the reported words state a universal truth or a habit that is still true, they stay in the simple present: The teacher said that the earth revolves around the sun. (3) If the situation is still true when you report it, the tense may be left unchanged, though back-shift is never wrong in an exam. (4) The past perfect and the modals would, could, should and might stay unchanged.

items.text: Direct: She said, 'I am tired.' Indirect: She said that she was tired.
Direct: Rita said, 'I have finished my work.' Indirect: Rita said that she had finished her work.
Direct: He said to me, 'Where do you live?' Indirect: He asked me where I lived.
items.note: Wh-question: statement order, no question mark.

items.text: Direct: Arun said to me, 'Can you swim?' Indirect: Arun asked me if I could swim.
items.note: Yes or no question: use if or whether; can becomes could.

items.text: Direct: The warden said to the boys, 'Do not run in the corridor.' Indirect: The warden told the boys not to run in the corridor.
items.note: Negative command: not to plus the base verb.

items.text: Direct: Mother said to me, 'I made these sweets yesterday.' Indirect: Mother told me that she had made those sweets the day before.
items.note: Tense, pronoun, this-that and time word all change.

items.text: Direct: Priya said, 'How beautiful the sunset is!' Indirect: Priya exclaimed that the sunset was very beautiful.
items.note: The exclamation becomes a statement. Priya exclaimed with delight that the sunset was very beautiful is also acceptable.

items.text: Direct: The teacher said, 'The earth revolves around the sun.' Indirect: The teacher said that the earth revolves around the sun.
items.note: A universal truth needs no back-shift.

learn.title: Common mistakes and how to correct them

items.text: Wrong: He said that he will come tomorrow. Right: He said that he would come the next day.
items.note: Past reporting verb: will becomes would and tomorrow changes.

items.text: Wrong: She asked me where was I going. Right: She asked me where I was going.
items.note: Use statement order in reported questions.

items.text: Wrong: He told that he was ill. Right: He said that he was ill. Or: He told me that he was ill.
items.note: Told needs a person; said does not.

items.text: Wrong: Mother told me do not touch it. Right: Mother told me not to touch it.
items.note: Commands use to plus base verb.

items.text: Wrong: He asked me that where I lived. Right: He asked me where I lived.
items.note: Do not add that in a wh-question.

items.text: Wrong: She asked did I like tea. Right: She asked whether I liked tea.
items.note: Yes or no questions need if or whether.

items.text: Wrong: The teacher said that the sun rose in the east. Right: The teacher said that the sun rises in the east.
items.note: A universal truth stays in the simple present.

items: Step 1. Decide the type of sentence inside the quotation marks: statement, question, command or exclamation.
Step 2. Choose the reporting verb that fits, and remove the quotation marks and comma.
Step 3. Check the tense of the reporting verb. If it is past, back-shift the reported words unless an exception applies.
Step 4. Change the pronouns by asking who is speaking, who is listening and who is reporting.
Step 5. Change time and place words and this or these.
Step 6. Use the correct joining word: that, if, whether, a wh-word or to.
Step 7. Reread. A reported question has no question mark and a reported statement is not a question in disguise.
For indirect to direct, reverse the steps and put the words back in quotation marks with a comma before them.

keyPoints: Direct speech quotes exact words; indirect speech reports them without quotation marks.
Four changes are needed: reporting verb, tense, pronouns, and time and place words.
Back-shift applies when the reporting verb is past; it does not apply when the reporting verb is present or future.
Universal truths and habitual facts stay in the simple present.
Reported questions use statement word order and no question mark.
Yes or no questions take if or whether; wh-questions keep their question word.
Commands and requests use to plus the base verb, or not to plus the base verb.
Exclamations are reported with exclaimed (with joy, sorrow or surprise) and a that clause.
examFocus: Converting direct speech into indirect speech and back.
Reporting questions, commands, requests and exclamations.
Changing pronouns and time and place words correctly.
Spotting errors in reported speech, especially word order and back-shift.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct indirect form of: She said, 'I am tired.'
options: She said that she is tired.
She said that she was tired.
She said that I was tired.
She said that she has been tired.
questions.answer: She said that she was tired.
questions.explanation: The reporting verb is past, so am becomes was, and I becomes she.
questions.commonMistake: Keeping the present tense after a past reporting verb.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct indirect form of: The teacher said, 'The earth revolves around the sun.'
options: The teacher said that the earth revolved around the sun.
The teacher said that the earth had revolved around the sun.
The teacher said that the earth revolves around the sun.
The teacher said that the earth would revolve around the sun.
questions.answer: The teacher said that the earth revolves around the sun.
questions.explanation: A universal truth stays in the simple present after a past reporting verb.
questions.commonMistake: Applying back-shift to a scientific fact.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct indirect form of: He said to me, 'Where do you live?'
options: He asked me where did I live.
He asked me where I lived.
He told me where I lived.
He asked me that where I lived.
questions.answer: He asked me where I lived.
questions.explanation: A wh-question is reported with asked, statement word order and no question mark. Told is used for statements, not questions.
questions.commonMistake: Keeping the question word order (did I live).

questions.prompt: In indirect speech after a past reporting verb, the word 'tomorrow' usually changes to:
questions.explanation: Tomorrow becomes the next day or the following day. The previous day is the change for yesterday.
questions.commonMistake: Mixing up the changes for yesterday and tomorrow.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: 'I have finished my work,' said Rita. Rita said that she ___ finished her work.
questions.explanation: The present perfect (have finished) becomes the past perfect (had finished) after a past reporting verb.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: 'Can you swim?' Arun asked me. Arun asked me ___ I could swim.
questions.explanation: A yes or no question is reported with if or whether. Both are correct.
questions.commonMistake: Using that or leaving the joining word out.

questions.prompt: Change into indirect speech: The warden said to the boys, 'Do not run in the corridor.'
questions.answer: The warden told the boys not to run in the corridor.
questions.explanation: A command is reported with told (or ordered, warned) and not to plus the base verb. Warned the boys not to run is also acceptable.
questions.commonMistake: Writing that they should not run without changing the form of the verb properly, or using do not.

questions.prompt: Change into indirect speech: Mother said to me, 'I made these sweets yesterday.'
questions.answer: Mother told me that she had made those sweets the day before.
questions.explanation: Said to becomes told; I becomes she; made becomes had made; these becomes those; yesterday becomes the day before (or the previous day).
questions.commonMistake: Forgetting to change these and yesterday.

questions.prompt: Change into indirect speech: 'Will you help me with this bag?' she said to him.
questions.answer: She asked him whether he would help her with that bag.
questions.explanation: The yes or no question uses whether or if. Will becomes would, you becomes he, me becomes her and this becomes that. She requested him to help her with that bag is also acceptable.
questions.commonMistake: Keeping the question order (would he help).

questions.prompt: Change into direct speech: The coach said that the team had played well the previous day.
questions.answer: The coach said, 'The team played well yesterday.'
questions.explanation: The previous day becomes yesterday and the past perfect goes back to the simple past. Quotation marks and a comma are needed.
questions.commonMistake: Keeping had played in the quotation while also writing yesterday.

questions.prompt: State two situations in which the tense of the reported words is not changed in indirect speech. Give an example of each.
questions.answer: First, when the reporting verb is in the present or future tense: He says, 'I am busy' becomes He says that he is busy. Second, when the reported words state a universal truth or a habitual fact: The teacher said, 'Water boils at 100 degrees Celsius' becomes The teacher said that water boils at 100 degrees Celsius.
questions.explanation: Credit for both situations and one example each. A third acceptable situation is a fact that is still true when reported.
questions.commonMistake: Back-shifting after a present reporting verb.

questions.prompt: Each sentence has one error in reported speech. Rewrite it correctly. (a) He said that he will come tomorrow. (b) She asked me where was I going. (c) He told that he was ill. (d) Mother told me do not touch it.
questions.answer: (a) He said that he would come the next day. (b) She asked me where I was going. (c) He said that he was ill. (or He told me that he was ill.) (d) Mother told me not to touch it.
questions.explanation: (a) Will becomes would and tomorrow changes to the next day. (b) A reported question has statement order. (c) Told needs a person as its object. (d) A command is reported with not to plus the base verb.
questions.commonMistake: Correcting the tense but leaving the time word unchanged.
